notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 24 compiled from the approved sources:

---

## Ezekiel 24 Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter has two main sections: **(1) The parable of the boiling pot (vv. 1–14)**, announcing the siege of Jerusalem, and **(2) the death of Ezekiel's wife as a sign (vv. 15–27)**, prefiguring how the exiles would respond to the fall of the temple. The date given (9th year, 10th month, 10th day) is authenticated by 2 Kings 25:1, Jeremiah 39:1, and Jeremiah 52:4. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html)

---

### v. 1: *"In the ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying,"*

This is the ninth year of Jehoiachin's captivity (which coincided with Zedekiah's reign), the month Tebet (late December/January), approximately 590 BC. The siege of Jerusalem lasted about two years from this date. — Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

---

### v. 2: *"Son of man, write down today's date, for on this very day the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem."*

Ezekiel was commanded to record the exact date so that when news later arrived confirming the prediction, the people would recognize him as a true prophet. The phrase "set himself against" is better rendered "has fallen upon." Ezekiel, hundreds of miles away in Chaldea, received this by direct revelation from God—not by ordinary human messengers. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

The date became so significant that the exiles later observed it as a fast day (Zechariah 8:19). — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html)

---

### vv. 3–5: The Parable of the Boiling Pot

**v. 3:** *"Now speak a parable to this rebellious house… 'Put the pot on the fire; put it on and pour in the water.'"*

This is not a symbolic action but a spoken parable, though the language sounds like action-description. The "pot" (or cauldron) is the same Hebrew word as in Ezekiel 11:3, where the people had boasted that the city was a protective cauldron. God now says: let it be so—but for judgment, not protection. The urgency is marked by the repeated command "set on." — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 4:** *"Put in the pieces of meat, every good piece—thigh and shoulder—fill it with choice bones."*

The "pieces" are literally "its pieces"—the pieces belonging to the cauldron, i.e., the people of Jerusalem. The "thigh and shoulder" and "choice bones" represent not only the leaders but all classes, even the best (princes, gentry, the mighty, the wealthy). During Nebuchadnezzar's campaign, people from the countryside fled into Jerusalem seeking safety, but this only gathered them for destruction. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 5:** *"Take the choicest of the flock and pile the fuel beneath it. Bring it to a boil and cook the bones in it."*

"The choice of the flock" means the king, princes, nobles, magistrates, and priests—the leaders. The "bones" piled under the pot is ambiguous: it could mean bones used as fuel (as attested by ancient practices; Livingstone used elephant bones as fuel for a steamer, notes Currey), or it could be a pile of bones for burning. Block argues that since the feminine plural form elsewhere in Ezekiel is used only of human bones, these are human bones—a chilling picture of the coming slaughter. — Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/)

---

### vv. 6–8: Woe to the Bloody City

**v. 6:** *"Woe to the city of bloodshed, to the pot now rusted, whose rust will not come off! Empty it piece by piece; cast no lots for its contents."*

Here the parable is explained: the "bloody city" is Jerusalem (cf. Nahum 3:1). The word translated "scum" (BSB: "rust") occurs five times in this chapter and nowhere else in Scripture; the old Greek version and nearly all interpreters agree it means "rust." The cauldron was made of copper/bronze (v. 11), so the rust was verdigris—the city itself is corroded by wickedness. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

"Bring it out piece by piece" means the inhabitants would be removed indiscriminately. "Cast no lots for its contents" means no discrimination would be made (unlike the Roman practice of decimating captives by lot)—all were doomed to death or exile. — Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 7:** *"For the blood she shed is still within her; she poured it out on the bare rock; she did not pour it on the ground to cover it with dust."*

Jerusalem had shed innocent blood openly and impudently, glorying in her crimes. The Mosaic law required that even the blood of animals slain for food be poured on the ground and covered with dust (Leviticus 17:13; Deuteronomy 12:16, 24). To leave blood exposed on bare rock was to flout God's law and to cry out for vengeance, like Abel's blood (Genesis 4:10). — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 8:** *"In order to stir up wrath and take vengeance, I have placed her blood on the bare rock, so that it would not be covered."*

God Himself now does what Jerusalem had done: He exposes her blood openly so that the punishment will be equally public. This is just retaliation—as her sin was open and unrepented, so her judgment will be open and unmistakable. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html)

---

### vv. 9–13: Further Woe and the Unsuccessful Cleansing

**v. 9:** *"Woe to the city of bloodshed! I, too, will pile the kindling high."*

The woe is repeated, echoing Nahum 3:1 (originally spoken against Nineveh). God will make the "pyre" (the pile of fuel) great—the army of the Chaldeans would be large, the siege severe, the carnage immense. — Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 10:** *"Pile on the logs and kindle the fire; cook the meat well and mix in the spices; let the bones be burned."*

"Spice it well" is better rendered "make thick the broth" (RV) or "boil thoroughly." The verb relates to the concoction of anointing oil (Exodus 30:33, 35) and its cognate describes boiling water in Job 41:31. The image is of a furious, thorough boiling until the water evaporates, the flesh is consumed, and even the bones burn. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 11:** *"Set the empty pot on its coals until it becomes hot and its copper glows. Then its impurity will melt within; its rust will be consumed."*

After the inhabitants (the meat) are removed, the empty cauldron—the depopulated city—is set back on the coals to be superheated. The fire will melt the copper and consume the rust. This is a symbolical purification under the law (Numbers 31:23), where defiled metal vessels were purified by fire. Here it means the destruction of the city itself. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 12:** *"It has frustrated every effort; its thick rust has not been removed, even by the fire."*

The phrase "she hath wearied herself with lies" is better rendered "it is worn out with labors"—the pains taken to cleanse the cauldron have been in vain; the rust remains. Even the fire of judgment has not sufficed to remove the deep-seated corruption. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 13:** *"Because of the indecency of your uncleanness I tried to cleanse you, but you would not be purified from your filthiness. You will not be pure again until My wrath against you has subsided."*

"Lewdness" (BSB: "indecency") denotes consummate wickedness joined with impudence—sins that are willful and deliberate, not accidental. God had used prophets, the temple, sacrifices, and even earlier chastisements (Josiah's reforms, Hezekiah's reforms) as cleansing agents, but all were rejected. Now only the fire of His wrath remained. Yet there is a glimmer of hope: when the punishment has done its full work, then God's fury will rest (cf. Ezekiel 16:42). — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

---

### v. 14: The Certainty of Judgment

*"I, the LORD, have spoken; the time is coming, and I will act. I will not refrain or show pity, nor will I relent. I will judge you according to your ways and deeds."*

This is the most emphatic affirmation of divine resolve in the book of Ezekiel. God piles up phrases to remove any doubt: He will not hold back, spare, or repent. The judgment is neither arbitrary nor excessive but exactly proportionate to their ways and deeds—under the covenant curses of Deuteronomy. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

The Pulpit Commentary's homiletic section notes that God's constancy, perfect knowledge, power, and mercy all guarantee His faithfulness to His word—both in threat and in promise. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

---

### vv. 15–17: The Death of Ezekiel's Wife Foretold

**v. 16:** *"Son of man, behold, I am about to take away the desire of your eyes with a fatal blow. But you must not mourn or weep or let your tears flow."*

"The desire of your eyes" is Ezekiel's wife—a tender phrase revealing the prophet's deep love and humanity beneath his austere exterior. The Hebrew word *magephoh* ("blow/stroke") can mean sudden death, plague, or disease (cf. 1 Samuel 4:17; Exodus 9:14). She would die suddenly, "with one stroke." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/); Constable (via excerpt)

Ezekiel was not forbidden to *feel* sorrow (even Jesus wept at Lazarus's grave), but he was forbidden from outward, loud manifestations of grief. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/)

John Piper (Reformed Baptist) sees the death of Ezekiel's wife as parallel to the apostolic pattern: "If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation" (2 Corinthians 1:6). The suffering of God's servants is an essential part of His judging and saving work. — Desiring God (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/ministry-after-god-takes-a-beloved-wife)

**v. 17:** *"Groan quietly; do not mourn for the dead. Put on your turban and strap your sandals on your feet; do not cover your lips or eat the bread of mourners."*

Each instruction reverses a normal mourning custom of the ancient Near East:
- **Turban on head**: Normally mourners removed their head-covering or covered the head with ashes/dust (2 Samuel 15:30).
- **Sandals on feet**: Mourners went barefoot (2 Samuel 15:30; Isaiah 20:2).
- **Do not cover your lips**: Mourners covered the lower face (Micah 3:7); lepers also did this (Leviticus 13:45).
- **Do not eat the bread of mourners**: Friends and neighbors customarily brought food to mourners (Jeremiah 16:7; Hosea 9:4). This "bread of men" (literally "bread of others") was part of a funeral feast. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

Regarding whether Ezekiel wore priestly garments: Ellicott notes that the special priestly garments were worn only when on duty within the tabernacle, so it is unlikely Ezekiel used them in captivity. The "turban" here was probably the ordinary head-covering. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html)

---

### vv. 18–19: The Death and the People's Question

**v. 18:** *"So I spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening my wife died. And the next morning I did as I had been commanded."*

What Ezekiel spoke in the morning was the parable of the boiling pot (vv. 3–14). Then the warning of his wife's death came, and she died that evening. The next morning, he appeared before the people showing no signs of mourning. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html)

Gill suggests Ezekiel told the people beforehand about the coming death so that when it occurred, they would see it as further proof of his prophetic authenticity. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that Ezekiel spent the day not at his wife's deathbed but in one last effort to impress God's word on hardened hearts—his prophetic calling superseded his natural human impulses. — Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 19:** *"Then the people asked me, 'Won't you tell us what these things you are doing mean to us?'"*

By this time the exiles were familiar with Ezekiel's method of symbolic actions. They realized his strange behavior must carry prophetic meaning and asked for an explanation. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/)

---

### vv. 20–24: The Sign Explained

**v. 21:** *"I am about to desecrate My sanctuary, the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and the delight of your soul. And the sons and daughters you left behind will fall by the sword."*

The temple is described in terms parallel to Ezekiel's wife: "the desire of your eyes," "the delight of your soul." The exiles had an irrational confidence in the mere existence of the temple, thinking God would never allow it to be destroyed. God would "profane" it—not merely by destruction but by allowing Gentiles to enter its most sacred precincts and carry off its treasures. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html)

"The sons and daughters whom you left behind" refers to family members of the exiles who remained in Judah and Jerusalem. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 22:** *"Then you will do as I have done: You will not cover your lips or eat the bread of mourners."*

As Ezekiel did not mourn his wife, so the exiles would not mourn the temple and their slain children. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/)

**v. 23:** *"Your turbans will remain on your heads and your sandals on your feet. You will not mourn or weep, but you will waste away because of your sins, and you will groan among yourselves."*

The grief would be too deep and stunning for outward expression. Some commentators suggest the Babylonian environment would also hinder public mourning. The "groaning among yourselves" indicates private, quiet expressions of pain, not the loud ritual wailing of normal funerals. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

"You shall pine away in your iniquities" echoes the covenant curse in Leviticus 26:39. This is not callousness but the beginning of repentance—they would mourn *for their iniquities*. — Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html)

**v. 24:** *"Thus Ezekiel will be a sign for you; you will do everything that he has done. When this happens, you will know that I am the Lord GOD."*

This is the only passage since Ezekiel 1:3 where the prophet names himself. His entire person—not just his actions—becomes a sign. The consistent purpose in Ezekiel is the revelation of God Himself through both tragedy and restoration. — Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-24.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/)

---

### vv. 25–27: The Promise of a Messenger and a Loosened Tongue

**v. 25:** *"And you, son of man, know that on the day I take away their stronghold, their pride and joy—the desire of their eyes which uplifted their souls—and their sons and daughters as well…"*

"Their stronghold" refers again to the temple—their false source of security. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/)

**v. 26:** *"on that day a fugitive will come and tell you the news."*

A survivor would escape from Jerusalem and bring word to the exiles in Babylon. This is fulfilled in Ezekiel 33:21, about three years later. — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/)

**v. 27:** *"On that day your mouth will be opened to him who has escaped; you will speak and no longer be mute. So you will be a sign to them, and they will know that I am the LORD."*

From the investment of Jerusalem until word of its fall (a period of about two years), Ezekiel gave no oral prophecy to the Israelites. He had foretold the result and now awaited it in silence. The prophecies he recorded against foreign nations (chapters 25–32) were written during this interval but apparently not spoken to the people. When the fugitive arrives, his mouth would be opened—and his ministry would shift from doom to hope and rebuilding (chapters 33–48). — Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/)

---

## Points of Difference Among Protestant Traditions

The sources I was able to consult within the search limits showed **broad agreement among Protestant commentators** on the meaning of this chapter. The following nuances emerged:

- **Reformed Baptist (John Piper / Desiring God):** Emphasizes that the suffering of God's servants—including Ezekiel's loss of his wife—is an integral part of God's judging and saving purposes, parallel to Paul's statement "death is at work in us, but life in you" (2 Corinthians 4:12). The afflicted minister becomes a sign and a means of grace to God's people. (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/ministry-after-god-takes-a-beloved-wife)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Highlights the supernatural revelation to Ezekiel—God supernaturally told him what was happening 300 miles away on the very day. Also emphasizes that Ezekiel, under the power of the Holy Spirit, was "not an absolute slave to his emotions" and could obey God despite devastating personal loss. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-24/)

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Stresses the precision of the historical dating and its corroboration with Kings and Jeremiah. Ellicott's approach is measured, scholarly, and focuses on textual detail (e.g., the Hebrew word for "rust," the sequence of events on the morning and evening). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-24.html)

- **Older Reformed Baptist (Gill):** Provides thorough doctrinal reflections, noting that God's sovereignty extends even to the death of a prophet's wife, and that the prohibition against mourning showed the judgment was beyond normal categories of grief. Gill emphasizes that the "stroke" may have been pestilence or a sudden apoplexy—death "by the hand of heaven." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-24.html)

---

## Catholic Reading

**Haydock's Catholic Bible Commentary** notes that Ezekiel was in Mesopotamia when the siege began, and the news arriving on that very day would confirm his prophetic authority. Haydock observes that the death of a beloved wife by pestilence or sudden death makes the loss more afflicting, yet such private calamities are swallowed up by public ones—a sentiment echoed from Seneca: *"Curæ leves loquuntur, graviores silent"* (light griefs speak; heavier ones are silent). Haydock also notes that "profane my sanctuary" means God would esteem it no more and abandon it to the Gentiles. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-24.html)

The **Catholic Encyclopedia** summarizes that Ezekiel 24 is the final chapter in the first part of Ezekiel (prophecies against Judah before the fall of Jerusalem). On the day the siege began, the prophet represented under the figure of "the rusty pot" what was to befall the city; and through the death of his wife, God taught the exiles that they should be willing to lose what is dearest to them without open grieving. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05737b.htm)

---

## Modern Scholarship

**Peake's Commentary** (via StudyLight excerpt) treats the chapter as the "last message before the fall of the city," delivered on the opening day of the siege. Peake views the parable as a "probably acted parable," where the pot filled with flesh represents the inhabitants (choice pieces = leaders). After boiling, the pieces are taken out in any order—symbolic of indiscriminate dispersion. The rust symbolizes blood shed in injustice and child sacrifice, which cries aloud for vengeance according to ancient Semitic ideas (Genesis 4:10). Peake also suggests that the first clause of v. 12 should probably be deleted. Regarding vv. 15–27, Peake notes that the prohibition of mourning customs includes covering the mustache (not "lips"), and that from v. 21 we learn that in the deportation of 597 BC some children were left behind. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-24.html)
